title: Decisions before wave 0
intro: The pilot decisions P1 to P4 are applied. Four calls remain before the contracts are frozen and wave 0 starts. Settled by checks and not asked: the Python 3.10 floor (uv ran 3.10.22) and the log-size default of 50 MB.

decisions.title: Which shared types wave 0 freezes
decisions.context: 47 names used in signatures are defined nowhere. 15 of them cross a module boundary (GateSpec and GateContext are used by seven modules), and 5 more shared types appear only in field lists. A type that two modules build to different shapes fails when they meet.

options.name: Freeze the 20 shared types now, with the shapes proposed in the review, and put them in section 18
pros: Every module in waves 1 to 3 codes to one shape
The shapes come from how callers already use each type, and the contract tests (W0.6) check them
The fakes can be written in wave 0
cons: Some shapes may be wrong until a module uses them; a change then touches every caller
About 28 module-local types still wait for their own wave

options.name: Freeze only the types section 18 already lists, plus Clock; each module defines the rest in its own wave
pros: Less written before any code exists
Each owner shapes its own types with its tests in hand
cons: The gap review shows the cross-module types (GateContext, PrRef, JoinResult) are the ones that mismatch
The fakes in wave 0 need those types, so they would be written against guesses

decisions.why: The types that cross modules are exactly where parallel builds fail, so fixing them first costs less than reconciling them later.

decisions.title: One configuration type or two
decisions.context: Module 3 defines `load_config(repo) -> Config` and merges machine and repo files into it. Module 16 calls `tick(cfg: MachineConfig, ...)`, and no module defines `MachineConfig`. `tick` runs with no repo, so `repo=None` is already allowed.

options.name: One Config with a machine part and a repo part; `tick` takes a Config loaded with repo=None
pros: No new type or loader
Precedence (flag, env, machine, repo, default) stays in one place
Matches module 3 as written; only module 16's signature changes
cons: A function that needs only machine settings can still be handed repo fields

options.name: Keep MachineConfig as its own type, with `load_machine_config` added to module 3
pros: The type says which settings a function may read
`tick` cannot read a repo setting by mistake
cons: A second loader, schema and set of tests
Functions that need both take two arguments

decisions.why: Module 3 already merges both files into one Config, so one type needs no new code.

decisions.title: Where the repo's worktree comparison comes from
decisions.ref: Module 17 `cleanup_check`; the pilot repo's AGENTS.md, section 3
decisions.context: The pilot repo's rule is to compare each changed file with the committed or merged file before a forced removal. It has no script that does this. With `cleanup_check` unset, every worktree that is not clean is skipped and reported, so they pile up until someone clears them. Untracked and ignored files have no committed copy to compare with.

options.name: The repo supplies the comparison as a command and sets `cleanup_check`; the spec stays as written
pros: The rule lives with the repo that owns it
No engine code that guesses what the rule means
Other repos with other rules use the same key
cons: The pilot skips every worktree that is not clean until it adds the script
Needs a change in the pilot repo, which you own

options.name: The factory ships a built-in comparison that checks changed tracked files against the run branch
pros: Works in the pilot at once
One implementation shared by every repo
cons: The engine decides what 'safe to remove' means, which is the repo's rule to set
It can only report untracked and ignored files, not judge them

options.name: No check at all: a worktree that is not clean is always kept, and you clear it by hand with `factory gc`
pros: Nothing is removed that was not compared by a person
No new key or code
cons: Drops the P2 decision you already took
Leftover worktrees and branches grow with every dirty run

decisions.why: P2 made the repo's comparison the gate, so the repo should provide it.

decisions.title: Worker isolation: how to stop a worker reading secrets
decisions.ref: Decision D7; module 9 threat model and isolation
decisions.context: D7 accepted a tool allowlist, a scrubbed environment and denied reads, with no OS sandbox (the spec says so in module 9 and the phase split). A canary test showed a Read deny rule blocks only the Read tool, and an allowed `python3` read the file anyway. Tested on macOS with Claude Code 2.1.325: its own sandbox setting (`sandbox.filesystem.denyRead`, `allowWrite`) blocked that read, and writes worked only in the worktree and the task folder. That setting runs each Bash command under `sandbox-exec` (seen in the process list), which the man page marks DEPRECATED; the binary also names `bwrap` for Linux. Not tested: Linux, and an OAuth login.

options.name: Turn on Claude Code's own sandbox setting for every worker, with denied reads for secrets and writes only to the worktree and `$FACTORY_TASK_DIR`; `doctor` runs the canary each time
pros: Tested: it blocks the interpreter read that beat the deny rule
Tested: writes to the worktree and task folder work; other paths are blocked
Anthropic keeps the sandbox profile, and the engine adds no wrapper code
cons: Claude only; a second harness in phase 2 needs its own boundary
On macOS it rests on `sandbox-exec`, which is marked DEPRECATED, so a future macOS can break it; `doctor` must prove it on each machine
The setting names can change between releases; Linux is not tested here

options.name: The factory wraps each worker itself: `sandbox-exec` on macOS and `bubblewrap` on Linux
pros: Same boundary for any harness, including Codex later
Tested on macOS: blocks both `python3` and `cat` reads of a denied file
The factory owns the profile, so a harness update cannot loosen it
cons: Same deprecated `sandbox-exec` on macOS, and the factory must maintain the profile
Two code paths to build and test, and `bubblewrap` is not tested here
More engine code in phase 1a

options.name: Keep D7 as accepted: allowlist and scrubbed environment only, with the open interpreter route reported by `doctor`
pros: No new code
Residual risk is already stated in module 9
cons: Tested: an allowed interpreter reads a denied file
A task allowed an interpreter can read your other secrets

decisions.why: It is the only option tested to close the gap without engine code, and both sandbox options rest on the same macOS mechanism, so the choice is who maintains it.
